massing: Model A1 (documented): a detached house whose roofline includes dormers; plan reorganised under Harold R. Wake so that a kitchen-family room replaces the separate dining and living rooms and adjoins two ground-floor bedrooms.
blurb_en: The first-phase house: one of the standard models of the summer of 1926, re-drawn by Wake to fit French-Canadian family life (a big kitchen instead of parlour and dining room), varied from house to house by dormers, porches and roof details so that, in the City's phrase, "not a single house was built that resembles its neighbour".
origin_en: Brainerd's New York-inspired type plans were "rationalised" on site by the engineer Harold R. Wake, who adapted them to Québec's climate and household size; the CPCQ dossier speaks of "quatre modèles types" enabling the 270 houses of 1926 in 135 days, with variety obtained through dormers, balconies and roofs. The address list is consistent with families A–D being that first set: on the 1926 streets almost every entry is an A, B, C or D code.

blurb_en: The founding house type of TMR. When Frederick Todd laid out the town in 1912 he was borrowing directly from Ebenezer Howard's Garden City movement, and the first houses near the station borrowed the movement's architecture too: the English Arts-and-Crafts cottage of Letchworth and Hampstead Garden Suburb. Look for steep 45° gables, a brick ground floor with stucco or half-timbering above, small-paned windows, and a deliberately picturesque, asymmetrical silhouette that reads as a cottage in a garden rather than a house on a street.
origin_en: The Garden City movement's architecture as well as its planning. Ebenezer Howard's 1898 tract produced Letchworth (Parker & Unwin, 1903) and Hampstead Garden Suburb (1907), and their house vocabulary, itself drawn from Voysey, Baillie Scott and the English cottage, travelled with the idea: steep gables, roughcast or half-timbered upper storeys over brick, small-paned casements, picturesque asymmetry, the house read as a cottage in a garden. The by-law's Garden City House is this, with the 45° roof, stucco-and-timber upper floor and small brick module written out as criteria.

blurb_en: “Faubourien” refers to the vernacular of Montreal's old inner suburbs (the faubourgs): a plain two-storey brick box, flat or hipped roof, sometimes a false mansard, and a front verandah on wooden columns. In TMR the type is what the Plateau or Rosemont row house becomes when it is given its own lot, a side driveway and a lawn. Its virtue is restraint: symmetry, aligned windows, one material.
origin_en: Faubourien points to the maison de faubourg, the plain brick house of Québec's nineteenth-century inner suburbs: two or three storeys, flat or false-mansard roof, aligned openings, minimal ornament, a front gallery on wooden posts. Montreal's Plateau PIIA uses the same term for its own housing stock. In TMR the type is what that urban house becomes on a detached or semi-detached lot with a side driveway; several examples take on the cubic mass and hipped roof of the American Foursquare, which was being built across Canada in the same years.

blurb_en: The interwar Montreal walk-up, three storeys of red brick under a flat roof, with a decorated parapet, a stone base, patterned brickwork and a prominent entrance portico. Balconies with iron or stone railings give the façade its rhythm. These sit on the town's few multi-family lots and are the collective sibling of the faubourg house.
origin_en: Three-storey brick apartment houses of the 1920s and 30s, Montreal's standard multi-family building of the period. This is where Art Deco actually lives in TMR: stepped and decorated parapets, geometric brick panels, artificial-stone entrance surrounds, iron balcony rails with angular motifs. Héritage Montréal describes the same repertoire on 1920s Montreal plexes (dark brick, artificial-stone insertions around doors and windows, appliqués with geometric forms). The by-law absorbs it as "distinctive brick motifs and bonds" and "a body crowned by a brick motif and a parapet" rather than naming the style.

blurb_en: A 1930s–50s revival of the 18th-century Quebec farmhouse: a steep roof whose eaves flare out into “larmiers” that shelter the front door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, and a calm symmetrical front. It was the domestic face of a broader interwar interest in Québécois heritage. The distinctive move is the roof, which is asked to express the base of the house through its overhang.
origin_en: A regionalist revival of the eighteenth-century Laurentian farmhouse: bell-cast roof whose eaves flare into larmiers sheltering the door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, a calm symmetrical front. The Canadian Encyclopedia locates its source in the anglophone rediscovery of pre-industrial Québec during the 1920s–30s, stimulated by Clarence Gagnon's paintings and encouraged by Percy Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair at McGill, whose surveys of old Québec buildings fed a fashion for fieldstone and pitched roofs among the province's leading domestic architects. TMR's Canadian houses are the suburban, builder-scale version of that fashion.

blurb_en: Colonial Revival as it arrived from the American Northeast: a long, simple gabled rectangle with its broad side to the street, symmetrical windows, dormers set halfway up the roof, and a discreet canopy over the front door. Brick or stone below, clapboard or stucco above. It is quieter than the Georgian house, and the by-law wants it kept quiet: bay windows are the only projections allowed.
origin_en: A long side-gabled rectangle with its broad face to the street, symmetrical openings, dormers half-way up the roof, a discreet door canopy; brick or stone below and clapboard or stucco above. It is the New England colonial house as codified in 1920s–40s pattern books and builders' plan services, the quieter cousin of Georgian Revival. The by-law keeps it quiet: bay windows are the only projections it allows.

blurb_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment courts arranged in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. A stone base and stone string courses tie them to the collegiate-Tudor mood of the interwar decades. Entrances are marked by a distinct architectural element rather than a big portico.
origin_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment blocks in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with stone bases, stone string courses, steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. The idiom is the residential cousin of interwar school and college architecture, and of the "garden apartment" courts built across North America in the 1930s–40s. The by-law's "New England (collective)" label is looser than the architecture: these blocks are more Tudor than New England.

blurb_en: Georgian Revival: the most formal of TMR's houses. A red-brick box of two full storeys, three or five bays wide, with a central door flanked by pilasters and topped by an elaborate crown, sash windows with small panes, and a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gabled roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law lets you emphasise the central bay with a slight projection and a pediment, and nothing more.
origin_en: The formal wing of Colonial Revival. Two full storeys of red brick, three or five bays, a central door with pilasters and an entablature or pediment, sash windows with small panes, a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gable roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law permits one flourish, a slightly projected central bay under a pediment, and nothing else. In Canada the style carried an Imperial-loyalist inflection that made it a natural fit for a town founded and first settled by anglophones.

blurb_en: Tudor Revival, TMR's most romantic type: steep 45° roofs broken into several gables, a natural-stone ground floor with brick or half-timbered stucco above, patterned brickwork (herringbone, Dutch bond), small-paned casements, sometimes a round turret at the entrance. Where the Georgian house is symmetrical, the manor is deliberately picturesque, and its garage is meant to hide.
origin_en: The by-law's "English manor" is Tudor Revival by any other name: stone ground floor with brick or stucco-and-timber above, patterned brick (herringbone, Dutch bond), 45° multi-gabled roofs, small-paned casements, sometimes a round entrance turret. In North America the style peaked in the 1920s–30s and lingered into the 1940s; its Montreal fashion was strongest in the anglophone west end and suburbs. Tudor detailing also surfaces on some Phase 1 Garden City houses, which is why the two types share the half-timbered gable.

blurb_en: The postwar ranch bungalow: one storey, long and low, with a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, and big undivided windows wider than they are tall. Buff (“chamois”) brick or stone, black shingles, a wide driveway. The type that arrived with the car and the last empty lots of the 1950s and 60s.
origin_en: One storey, long and low, a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, big undivided windows wider than tall, buff ("chamois") brick or stone, a wide driveway. In Québec usage bungalow simply means the postwar single-family suburban house; the form is the Ranch house that spread from the American Southwest after 1945 and became the default Canadian suburban dwelling of the 1950s–60s.

style_label: Postwar two-storey (Québec cottage), with Minimal Traditional and Moderne notes
siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Wide driveway | Pedestrian path joins the driveway | Front setback of about 12 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 2.5 m | Typical lot width 20–25 m
massing: Simple volumes of two full storeys | Typical width of 15 m per semi-detached unit, 16 m for a detached house | Garage integrated into the volume, in the façade | Entrance sheltered by a marquise
articulation: A base distinguished by a dividing line at the ground-floor window lintels or the upper-floor window sills | Four-slope roofs of low pitch (30°)
openings: Glazing without small panes | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Horizontal window proportion (width = twice the height)
materials: Natural stone or red clay brick on the ground floor | Stucco or clapboard on the upper floor | Black asphalt shingles, or a tone matched to the cladding colour
blurb_en: In Quebec usage a “cottage” is simply a two-storey detached house, and this is its postwar version: a plain box under a low hip roof, stone or brick on the ground floor with stucco or siding above, garage built into the front, and a flat marquise over the door. A visible line at the ground-floor lintels or the upper sills divides base from body.
origin_en: In Québec real-estate usage a cottage is a two-storey detached house, as opposed to the one-storey bungalow; the OQLF notes the word's British origin and its earlier sense of an elegant, English-inspired country house. TMR's postwar cottage is a plain box: stone or brick base, stucco or siding above, low hip roof, integrated garage, flat marquise over the door, a horizontal line at the ground-floor lintels or upper sills dividing base from body. Some examples keep vestigial colonial detailing (Minimal Traditional); others, in cut stone with flat roofs and rounded or banded corners, are the town's clearest echo of Streamline Moderne.

siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Wide driveway | Pedestrian path joins the driveway | Front setback of about 12 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 2.5 m | Typical lot width 20–25 m
massing: Recessed entrance protected by the roof overhang | Attic additions and alterations respect the massing | Garage integrated into the volume and projecting from the façade
articulation: Composition in two vertical sections, one of one storey and the other of one and a half storeys | A base expressed on the one-and-a-half-storey volume, continuous with the level of the one-storey part | Two- or four-slope roofs of low pitch (30°) | Typical width of 15 m per semi-detached unit and 15 m for a detached house
openings: Glazing without small panes | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Horizontal window proportion (width = twice the height)
materials: Salmon, buff, brown or sand natural stone; wood or metal cladding for infill elements | Black asphalt shingles, or a tone matched to the main cladding | Same roofing material on both sections | A light cladding (wood, aluminium, composite or acrylic) may be used for architectural elements
blurb_en: Two volumes offset by half a storey: a one-storey wing beside a one-and-a-half-storey wing, with the garage tucked under the bedrooms and pushed forward, and a recessed entrance under the eaves. Salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels; both roofs share one low-pitched material. The interior stair does the work the façade shows.
origin_en: A plan type more than a style, dominant across North American suburbs from the mid-1950s: two volumes offset by half a storey, the garage under the bedrooms and pushed forward, a recessed entrance under the eaves. TMR's are dressed in Ranch and Contemporary materials, salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels, under one shared low-pitched roof.

siting_landscape: At least 60 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Wide driveway | Pedestrian path joins the driveway | Front setback of about 12 m from the sidewalk; side setbacks of about 2.5 m | Typical lot width 20–25 m
massing: Asymmetrical composition | Simple volumes of two full storeys | One-storey porch or secondary volumes (garage, solarium, etc.) that reinforce the horizontality
articulation: A base ending below the upper-floor window sills | Horizontality reinforced by the details | Low-pitched (30°) pyramidal or multi-slope roofs with deep soffits | Typical width of 15 m for both semi-detached and detached units
openings: Windows subdivided horizontally, without small panes | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Upper-floor windows directly under the horizontal soffit line | Ribbon windows that may wrap the corners of volumes | Horizontal window proportion (width > height)
materials: Brownish-red clay brick or natural stone | Elongated “Roman” brick module, or long cut stone | A light material (wood, aluminium, composite or acrylic) may be used in gables and above the base | Dark asphalt shingles, or a tone matched to the main cladding
blurb_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom, filtered through 1960s Montreal: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked right under the eaves and running around the corners as ribbons, long “Roman” brick or long-cut stone, and one-storey wings (garage, porch, solarium) that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical, and the most architect-driven of the phase-3 types.
origin_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom of 1900–1915, revived and simplified in the 1950s–60s Contemporary house: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked under the eaves and wrapping the corners as ribbons, long "Roman" brick or long-cut stone, one-storey wings that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical and the most architect-driven of the Phase 3 types; the by-law's insistence on the Roman brick module is the tell.

siting_landscape: At least 95 % of the front yard kept as vegetation | Basement parking garage at the rear or side, reached from a lane
massing: Simple, horizontal volumes | Entrance sheltered by a marquise | Main volume crowned by a set-back penthouse storey
articulation: Balconies grouped in loggias | Flat roof with a horizontal coping band
openings: Glazing without small panes | Bay windows may be added if they respect the type | Horizontal window proportion (width = 2.5 times the height)
materials: Clay brick in a sand or red tone | A variety of brick colours
blurb_en: The 1950s–70s modernist apartment building: flat roof finished with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor on top, balconies grouped into recessed loggias, wide undivided windows and a marquise over the door. Sand or red brick, often several brick colours on one façade. Parking goes underground; the front yard stays almost entirely green.
origin_en: Flat-roofed brick slabs of the 1950s–70s with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor, loggia balconies and wide undivided windows, in sand or red brick and often several brick colours on one façade. The town's share of the postwar Modernism that lines Côte-des-Neiges and Sherbrooke; the earliest examples, with brick-and-stone banding, still carry a Streamline accent.

source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, family 1 (fiche not retrieved); Étude typomorphologique 2003
blurb_en: The oldest surviving houses of the villages, small attached workers' houses at the street line.
origin_en: Villages period, 1845–1880; the earliest built layer of the borough.

siting_landscape: Front setback that may exceed 5 metres; small side setbacks of 1 to 2 metres. | Oldest examples (1850–1880) on rue Sherbrooke; from the 1900s, rarely, on rue Saint-Hubert, rue Rachel and avenue du Parc-La Fontaine. Many converted to offices or flats.
massing: Centred door; a projecting element may form an oriel or forebody. No sub-variant.
materials: Uniform stone cladding and a higher degree of ornamentation than the duplex (family description).
blurb_en: The bourgeois villa of the Plateau's first decades: a free-standing stone house set back from the street, individually designed, now rare and often converted.
origin_en: Built for the well-to-do west of Saint-Laurent and south of avenue des Pins, then along Sherbrooke, Square Saint-Louis and Saint-Hubert; the family also includes a two-unit superposed variant that differs from the duplex by storeys per dwelling, uniform stone facing and richer ornament.

name_fr: Le duplex sans marge de recul avant
siting_landscape: Party-wall building with no front or side setback. | The base type from which the other duplex variants derive; oldest subdivisions (Ferme Bagg, Courville, Ferme Comte, rue Pontiac, rue Drolet, Village des Carrières).
massing: Rectangular body without projections, two storeys very slightly raised above grade, flat roof. | Possibly a small balcony above the entrance doors (rarely more than one third of the façade width). | Upper dwelling reached by an interior stair.
articulation: Base of the building marked by one or two courses of rusticated stone. | Paired doors at one end of the façade; openings aligned vertically and horizontally; no significant variation in the choice or placement of cladding. | Crown formed by a moulded cornice, more or less elaborate.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins, with or without transom. | Doors with or without transom; transom height about one quarter to one fifth of the door. | Lintels of dressed stone or of soldier-course clay brick; on rusticated-stone buildings the surrounds are dressed stone and the lintel is often absorbed into a band running the width of the façade.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional rusticated stone cladding.
blurb_en: The plainest and oldest plex: two superposed flats in a brick box built right on the sidewalk line, paired front doors at one end, an interior stair to the upper flat, and a moulded cornice as the only crown. Its three sub-variants add a small entrance balcony, rusticated stone facing, or a porte cochère.
origin_en: The duplex was the first housing type built in the borough under the large speculative subdivisions of the 1880s and belongs to the first construction boom of 1885–1891. It is the developer's product of the pre-1880 regime, before Montréal imposed the front setback: a simple rectangle of two flats, one over the other, that the later duplexes and the triplex all descend from.
photo_credit: pending: extract from Annexe C / fiche 2.1

name_fr: Le duplex avec marge de recul avant
style_label: Montréal faubourg vernacular / Second Empire / mansard / Victorian eclecticism
siting_landscape: Front setback of 1 to 2 metres.
massing: Rectangular body without projections; two storeys with the ground floor raised fewer than 8 risers above grade; flat roof; balcony generally present above the entrance porch. | Occasional front gallery on the ground floor and sometimes the upper floor; small straight entrance stair. | Frequent use of a false-mansard roof.
articulation: Base marked by courses of rusticated stone. | Paired doors at one end of the façade; openings aligned vertically and horizontally. | On flat-roofed buildings, crown marked by a moulded cornice; on false-mansard buildings, pedimented or round-arched dormers generally aligned with the wall plane, the dormer over the balcony often raised to form a stronger crown above the entrance axis.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins, with or without transom; proportion 1 width = ½ height. | Doors with or without transom; transom about one quarter of the door height. | Lintels expressed by a dressed-stone band or a soldier course of clay brick.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional rusticated stone cladding.
blurb_en: The same two-flat box pulled back a metre or two from the sidewalk, which is enough to raise the ground floor a few steps, hang a balcony over the porch and, very often, top the façade with a false mansard and dormers. This is the duplex most people picture: the one with the mansard.
origin_en: Around 1880 Montréal began applying building by-laws to the new districts: standardised lots and lanes, then a mandatory front setback and stone or brick cladding. The setback produced this variant. Its false-mansard crown is the Second Empire fashion of the 1870s–80s applied to a speculative type; the mansard is decorative (a fausse mansarde), not a full storey.

siting_landscape: With a front setback. | Mainly in the landscape units of the east and north of the borough.
massing: Rectangular body without projections; two storeys with the ground floor raised 1 to 4 risers; flat roof; upper-floor balcony and exterior stair to reach the upper flat.
articulation: Foundation little marked; cladding may change between ground floor and upper floor. | Horizontal symmetry: an axis of doors at the centre with an axis of windows on each side; openings aligned horizontally. | Crown marked by a moulded cornice or a parapet with or without pediment.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins and without transom; proportion 1 width = ½ height; a few square windows with fixed or sliding panels. | Doors with or without transom; transom less than a quarter of the door height. | Lintel of dressed stone or soldier-course clay brick.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional stone cladding.
blurb_en: Two flats, but the upper one now has its own door and its own stair climbing the front of the house. The façade turns symmetrical, doors in the middle, windows either side, and the cornice can give way to a brick parapet. It is the duplex learning the triplex's trick.
origin_en: Built from the same moment as the triplex (type 3.2) and the multiplex (3.3), i.e. the second boom of 1904–1914. The exterior stair is the direct consequence of the mandatory front setback: with the building pushed back, the stair to the upper dwelling could be moved outside and the interior floor area given back to the flats.

source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 3.1 (not yet retrieved); Étude typomorphologique 2003
blurb_en: The rare early triplex whose stair is still inside: three flats behind one door, built before the front-setback rule pushed the stair outdoors.
origin_en: Transitional form of c. 1880 between the duplex and the exterior-stair triplex, per the Étude typomorphologique.

source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 3.2 (fiche not yet retrieved); Étude typomorphologique 2003; unité de paysage 4.7 fiche
siting_landscape: Front setback; rectangular plan occupying almost the whole parcel, or an inverted L-plan mirrored from one building to the next; twin buildings on two parcels often read as one.
massing: Three storeys; ground floor raised 0 to 5 risers; flat roof; exterior stair to the upper dwellings. | Occasional narrow balconies on the second and third levels; projecting bay windows are rare.
materials: Clay brick in beige or brown tones; stair and balcony with wood floors and metal railings.
blurb_en: The Montréal triplex: three flats stacked in a three-storey brick front, the upper two reached by an outside stair, often the famous curving iron one, with balconies at each level and an L-shaped footprint that leaves a light-well at the back. It is the dominant building of the borough.
origin_en: The Étude typomorphologique calls the triplex "la forme architecturale typique de ce secteur de Montréal" and dates it to the second boom, 1904–1914, driven by housing demand and by municipal regulation: standard lots and lanes (1880), then the mandatory front setback and stone or brick cladding, which "amènera la translation de l'escalier d'accès aux logements des étages supérieurs vers l'extérieur". Réjean Legault (1989) is the standard scholarly account.

source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 3.3 (not yet retrieved); Étude typomorphologique 2003
blurb_en: Three storeys, more than three flats; the plex scaled up.
origin_en: Same boom as the exterior-stair triplex, 1904–1914.

style_label: Victorian eclecticism / Second Empire / mansard / Queen Anne
blurb_en: Terraced bourgeois houses in stone, homogeneous by row, around Square Saint-Louis and along Cherrier and Saint-Hubert.
origin_en: Golden-age product for the middle class, 1885–1914; the study's "demeures bourgeoises".

siting_landscape: Concentrated on boulevard Saint-Joseph and avenue du Parc.
massing: Compact volume | without interior court.
materials: Foundation in stone or exposed concrete. No sub-variant.
blurb_en: The interwar prestige apartment building in its compact form.
origin_en: The opening of the great boulevards in the first half of the twentieth century allowed high-density prestige housing; the édifices de rapport appeared mostly between the two wars on Saint-Joseph and avenue du Parc, in two variants distinguished by the presence or absence of an interior court.

siting_landscape: Front setback varying from 0 to 5 metres, but the recessing of part of the façade creates a court open to the street of variable depth. | Large parcels; concentrated on avenue du Parc.
massing: Plan generally in a U; three or four storeys; ground floor generally raised. | Much larger bulk and dwelling count than the courtless variant.
blurb_en: The U-plan apartment court of avenue du Parc, its forecourt open to the street.
origin_en: Same interwar moment as the compact block, on larger parcels.

siting_landscape: Mainly in the landscape units Rues Messier et Parthenais (5.4) | Rue d'Iberville (5.5) and Rue Saint-Hubert Nord (5.9).
massing: Volume similar to the duplex; two to four dwellings reached from an interior stair.
blurb_en: A duplex-sized box holding two to four flats off one inside stair; postwar, and rare in the borough.
origin_en: Appeared mainly after the Second World War; little used in the Plateau. Post-1945 apartment buildings in general were replacement buildings built one by one across the territory, "une rupture importante avec le paysage urbain existant", often on vacant land along the railway.

phase_title: French tradition — riverside farms of Mouillepied
name_fr: La maison traditionnelle française et québécoise
siting_landscape: The oldest current in Saint-Lambert; the French-tradition model covers the 18th and early 19th century (1700–1830), the Québécois synthesis about 1830–1880. | Former farmhouses that once lined the St. Lawrence.
massing: Rectangular body of one and a half storeys, little raised above the ground. | Two-slope roof, straight or with a curved base, fairly steep. | Full-length wood gallery on the main façade, sheltered by the roof's eave (larmier); massive stone chimneys at the roof ends.
articulation: Ornament is spare; often the only decorative element is a wooden surround (chambranle) around the openings, painted in a colour contrasting with the walls. | British influence shows in the curved roof extension, more openings, rigorous symmetry, the front gallery and classical decorative touches.
openings: Traditional wood doors with glazing. | Two-leaf wood casements with 12 to 24 small panes or 6 large panes. | Small gabled dormers.
materials: Stone walls (French tradition); roughcast or wood. | Roof: traditional sheet metal (à baguettes, à la canadienne, pincée) or cedar shingle.
conservation: No imitation stone; do not paint masonry; replace roughcast or wood with identical material; industrial materials (aluminium, vinyl, wood composite, fibre cement) proscribed. | Asphalt shingle, industrial-looking sheet metal and synthetics proscribed on the roof. | Do not remove or narrow the gallery; railings in painted wood of traditional make, not metal or prefab-look treated wood. | Steel or PVC doors unsuitable; avoid guillotine, sliding, single-leaf crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows (a wood crank window imitating the large-pane casement is acceptable); do not add dormers to a roof that has none. | Do not raise foundations or change roof pitch; enlarge at the side or rear, reduced in volume, same roof form, set back from the front; never in front or flush with the main façade. | Do not overload with decorative elements.
blurb_en: The oldest houses in town: low stone farmhouses under a steep gable, later "quebecised" with a flared eave, more windows, a symmetrical front and a gallery. Almost nothing decorates them beyond a painted wooden surround, and the fiche wants it kept that way.
origin_en: The French-regime rural house of the seigneurie of La Prairie de la Magdeleine (the riverside strip known as Mouillepied), and its 19th-century synthesis with English neoclassicism, the maison traditionnelle québécoise, which "domine le paysage bâti … de 1830 à 1880 environ". Houses built under the French regime were often altered later to take on the Québécois traits.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 1

name_en: Mansard-roofed house of Second Empire influence
name_fr: La maison à mansarde d'influence Second Empire
siting_landscape: Well represented in Saint-Lambert over a long period, about 1875 to 1925; variants with two- or four-slope mansards, semi-detached pairs, and from the early 20th century a gable-to-street model; some dressed up as bourgeois houses with turrets and gables.
massing: Rectangular body of two storeys, moderately raised above the ground; mansard (broken) roof with two or four slopes; the gable wall may face the street. | Wood gallery sheltered by an awning independent of the main roof; a brick chimney generally on the roof.
articulation: Decorative woodwork on the gallery, the dormers and the roof edges; on wood- or light-clad houses, chambranles around openings and corner boards.
openings: Traditional wood doors with glazing. | Two-leaf wood casements with six large panes, or guillotine windows. | Dormers of various shapes piercing the steep lower slope (brisis).
materials: Brick, roughcast or wood walls. | Roof: traditional sheet metal (à baguettes, pincée, à la canadienne) or slate; galvanised traditional metal can be repaired and repainted.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; identical replacement for roughcast/wood; industrial claddings proscribed; asphalt shingle, industrial-look metal and synthetics proscribed on the roof. | Do not remove or resize the gallery; painted wood railings of traditional make. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable; avoid sliding, single-leaf crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or change roof pitch; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: Two storeys under a mansard: the steep lower slope carries the dormers, the gallery has its own little roof, and the woodwork on dormers and eaves is where the money went. Sometimes the gable turns to face the street; sometimes a turret makes it bourgeois.
origin_en: Second Empire (Napoléon III, 1852–70) reached North America through the United States around 1870, first on public buildings, then on prosperous houses, then on modest ones for which "son influence se limite au toit mansardé", a roof whose broken slopes give more room upstairs for large families.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 2

name_fr: La maison de style Queen Anne
siting_landscape: A strong presence in Saint-Lambert; the influence begins in the 1890s and persists to the early 1930s. Few perfect examples, many houses, detached or semi-detached, borrowing its elements.
massing: Rectangular or irregular plan of two and a half storeys, moderately raised; two- or four-slope roof of medium pitch; detached or semi-detached. | Asymmetrical façade articulated by numerous projections: towers, turrets, gables, oriels, bays, galleries, verandas, porches; wood gallery and porch under an awning.
articulation: Elaborate ornament drawing on the classical and picturesque repertoires: classical columns or piers, pediments and worked railings on the gallery; gables and turrets on the roof; cornices underlining the eaves; wood shingle cladding sometimes in decorative patterns.
openings: Traditional wood doors with glazing. | Wood casements, sometimes with transom, or guillotine windows. | Dormers of various models.
materials: Brick, or wood (clapboard or shingle). | Roof: traditional sheet metal or slate; industrial metal acceptable only if screws are hidden and it recalls traditional metal.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; identical replacement for wood cladding; industrial claddings proscribed; asphalt shingle and synthetics proscribed on the roof. | Railings in painted wood or wrought iron of traditional make; oriels, gables and bays maintained with care. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or change pitches; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: The town's signature Victorian: turrets, gables, oriels, a columned gallery, patterned shingles, everything asymmetrical and everything ornamented. Rarely textbook-pure in Saint-Lambert, but its vocabulary is everywhere on the streets laid out after 1889.
origin_en: One of the late-Victorian eclectic currents (with neo-Gothic, neo-Romanesque, neo-Tudor, neo-Renaissance), named after Queen Anne Stuart's reign (1665–1714) and characterised by "effets ornementaux d'inspiration pittoresque et classique". Its Saint-Lambert examples (Maison Desaulniers 1909, Maison O'Neill 1913) belong to the Anglo-Protestant streetcar-suburb build-out.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 3

name_fr: La maison Boomtown à fausse mansarde
siting_landscape: A Montréal model that enjoyed real popularity in Saint-Lambert on detached and semi-detached houses; fades from the 1910s in favour of plainer buildings.
massing: Rectangular body of two storeys, moderately raised; flat or gently rear-sloping roof with a false mansard as crown; detached or semi-detached. | Wood gallery under an awning independent of the main roof; verandas and oriels also in wood.
articulation: Second Empire décor confined to the crown, with elaborate woodwork: pendant dormers half in the wall and half in the false mansard, ornamented like the cornice and the gallery. | Decorative woodwork on the gallery (worked piers, railings, brackets) and on the dormers; a cornice usually marks the base of the false mansard; chambranles and corner boards on wood-clad houses; uniformity between the two units of a semi-detached pair.
openings: Traditional wood doors with glazing. | Two-leaf wood casements with six large panes, or guillotine windows. | Pendant gabled dormers piercing the false mansard, often elaborately ornamented.
materials: Brick, roughcast or wood walls. | False mansard in traditional sheet metal (à baguettes, pincée, en plaques) or slate.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; identical replacement for roughcast/wood; industrial claddings proscribed; asphalt shingle, industrial metal and synthetics proscribed on the false mansard. | Do not remove or resize the gallery; painted wood railings of traditional make; verandas and oriels in wood. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or alter the false mansard's dimensions; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: A flat-roofed brick house wearing a mansard as a hat. Montréal builders bolted the steep lower slope of a Second Empire roof onto the front of a cheap Boomtown box, hung dormers half in the wall and half in the slope, and dressed the lot in turned wood. It sits at the head of the Boomtown family and links Saint-Lambert to Mount Royal's "maison faubourienne".
origin_en: "Un amalgame intéressant entre la construction à toit plat avec couronnement et l'habitation à mansarde d'influence Second Empire": from the late 19th century Montréal contractors combined the modernity and low cost of the flat-roofed Boomtown house with the elegance of the mansard, plating the brisis onto the façade as a crown. Like the true mansard house it ran out of steam from the 1910s.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 4

name_en: Boomtown house with crown (parapet or cornice)
siting_landscape: Very present in Saint-Lambert; covers 1900 to 1930, the period of the town's main growth. Detached, semi-detached and terrace houses.
massing: Rectangular body of two storeys, moderately raised; flat or gently rear-sloping roof finished with a crown, parapet or cornice; detached or semi-detached. | Wood gallery or porch under an awning; oriels or projecting bays may replace the gallery.
articulation: Ornament concentrated in the crown of the façade: prominent worked cornices, or brick parapets of many forms, stepped, gabled, cut out, or patterned with brickwork. | Woodwork on galleries and porches: worked piers, railings, brackets.
openings: Wood doors with glazing. | Wood casements or guillotine windows according to the original model.
materials: Brick (no imitation, unpainted); wood elsewhere.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; identical wood replacement; industrial claddings proscribed. | Railings in painted wood or wrought iron of traditional make. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or add a pitched roof; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: The plain workers' box of the industrial city, two storeys of brick under a flat roof, whose only vanity is its top edge: a fat cornice or a brick parapet, stepped, gabled, cut or patterned. What Mount Royal's by-law calls the faubourg house is this building on a suburban lot.
origin_en: "Typiquement américain", devised in the late 19th century to house workers fast and cheaply in the boom towns of the industrial United States; originally a low rear-sloping roof hidden by parapet or cornice, generalised to a true flat roof once roofing technology allowed, in the early 20th century.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 5

siting_landscape: Appeared in the United States at the end of the 19th century and took hold in Québec in the first decades of the 20th; numerous in Saint-Lambert; variants from wealthy families' residences to semi-detached pairs for the middle class.
massing: Square or rectangular body of two storeys, slightly raised; pyramidal four-slope (pavilion) or hipped roof; detached or semi-detached. | Projections may be added: forebodies, oriels, entrance vestibules; wood gallery or porch under an awning; oriels, verandas and gables in their traditional material.
articulation: Ornament rather sober: decorative woodwork on gallery or porch, brick patterns, exposed rafter ends (chevrons) at the base of the roof.
openings: Wood doors with glazing, with or without transom. | Wood casements or guillotine windows, with or without muntins, per the original. | Hipped or shed (rampantes) dormers.
materials: Almost always brick. | Roof: traditional sheet metal preferred; asphalt shingle acceptable if original.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; keep brick and mortar sound; industrial claddings proscribed; on the roof, plastic and other synthetics proscribed. | Railings in painted wood or wrought iron of traditional make. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable unless perfect imitations; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or change pitches; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: The Four Square: a big brick cube under a pyramid roof, roomy enough for large families, cheap enough because its parts came by catalogue. Sober by nature; the porch woodwork, a brick pattern and the exposed rafter tails are its ornaments.
origin_en: Product of standardised materials and prefabricated components orderable by catalogue, hence "abordable et facile à construire", popular in village, town and country alike in the first decades of the 20th century.

name_en: House of Arts and Crafts influence
name_fr: La maison d'influence Arts and Crafts
style_label: Arts and Crafts / Craftsman / Shingle Style
siting_landscape: Found here and there in Saint-Lambert, built in the first half of the 20th century; American models carry the picturesque movement locally.
massing: One-and-a-half-storey body with an articulated plan (projections and forebodies) and pitched roofs of varied shapes and unequal slope lengths. | Several covered projections, galleries, balconies, porches, verandas, on all façades; gables, turrets, oriels and bays frequent; a generously sized gallery.
articulation: Sober ornament: chambranles and corner boards on wood-clad houses; traditional structural members (half-timbering, rafters) used as ornament; galleries with worked posts and brackets.
openings: Wood doors with glazing, with or without transom. | Wood casements or guillotine windows, with or without muntins, varied in shape and size. | Dormers of varied models.
materials: Brick, roughcast, cedar shingle or wood clapboard. | Roof: traditional sheet metal preferred; cedar shingle, tile and asphalt shingle acceptable.
conservation: Natural materials only; no imitation; industrial claddings and plastic proscribed. | Wood projections maintained and repainted; ornament kept or reproduced; do not overload, "la sobriété reste de mise". | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable unless perfect imitations; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or change pitches; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: Low, broad and shingled or roughcast, with a roof that breaks into different slopes and a porch big enough to live on. Ornament is the structure itself: exposed rafters, a bit of half-timbering, brackets under the porch roof. Scattered rather than clustered in Saint-Lambert.
origin_en: Arts and Crafts (Morris, Ruskin) reached the United States and merged with Shingle Style and Craftsman, spread by mail-order plan catalogues; in Montréal it produced a return of English house types and of New France forms, but "à Saint-Lambert, ce sont les modèles américains qui perpétuent le mouvement pittoresque". Cousin of Mount Royal's Garden City house, hence the shared canonical type.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 7

name_fr: L'immeuble à logements multiples de type plex
siting_landscape: Early 20th-century densification model imported from Montréal by developers; usually party-wall, may be semi-detached (quadruplex, quintuplex) or repeated in rows.
massing: Rectangular body of two or three storeys, moderately raised, flat roof. | Almost always superposed galleries and balconies on the main façade and, for plexes, exterior stairs; oriels or projecting bays may articulate the façade. | Some multi-dwelling buildings have shared entrances or stairs serving several units; usually three storeys, with galleries and balconies so each family has private outdoor space.
articulation: Ornament concentrated in the crown: cornices, parapets of various forms, brick patterns; woodwork (worked piers, railings, brackets) on galleries and balconies; ornament varies with the intended tenants.
openings: Wood doors with glazing. | Guillotine windows.
materials: Brick (no imitation, unpainted).
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; keep brick and mortar sound. | Do not remove galleries, balconies or stairs or change their dimensions; railings in painted wood or wrought iron of traditional make, uniform on all projections. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable unless perfect imitations; avoid sliding and single-leaf crank windows and undivided windows. | Do not raise foundations or add a pitched roof; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: The Montréal plex on the South Shore: stacked flats behind stacked galleries, outside stairs, a brick crown of cornice or parapet. Saint-Lambert's version is the fiche's own summary of what the Plateau's typology splits into duplex, triplex and multiplex.
origin_en: "La densification des villes, au début du 20e siècle, entraîne la prolifération d'immeubles à logements multiples … une forme d'habitation populaire se développe à grande échelle à Montréal : le plex", whose success in certain Montréal districts led promoters to build it in Saint-Lambert. For the type's genesis in the 1880s by-laws see the Plateau-Mont-Royal page.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 9

phase_title: Interwar catalogue houses and the King Cottage
source_ref: Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 8; Étude spécifique sur les maisons de Francis King (Sept. 2019)
siting_landscape: Very frequent in the Saint-Lambert landscape; built by contractor Francis King between 1932 and 1951 (70 to 100 houses), concentrated in the sectors suited to the middle and upper-middle class (Brooklyn Park and around); the oldest sector south of Victoria has one, his own at 44 rue Argyle.
massing: Square or rectangular body of two storeys, slightly raised; two-slope or hipped roof; generally detached. | Several gables; a portal, porch or portico topped by a gable marks the main entrance.
articulation: Rather sober: decorative woodwork on the portal or porch, false half-timbering in the gables, brick patterns; pale colours for accent materials.
openings: Wood doors with or without glazing. | Wood casements with diamond leading (résilles en losange). | Gabled dormers often half engaged in roof and wall (pendant dormers).
materials: Brick. | Roof: dark asphalt shingle, the original material.
conservation: No imitation brick; do not paint masonry; keep brick and mortar sound; industrial claddings proscribed. | Projections and gables keep their traditional material. | Steel/PVC doors unsuitable unless perfect imitations of the original; avoid sliding, crank, undivided, aluminium or PVC windows. | Do not raise foundations or change pitches; enlarge or add a garage at the side or rear, reduced in volume, same roof form, set back; never in front.
blurb_en: Saint-Lambert's own house: a two-storey brick cottage with several gables, a gabled porch, a little false half-timbering, diamond-leaded casements and dormers half sunk into the eave, built by the hundred by one contractor between the Depression and 1951, and named for him only in the 1980s.
origin_en: Francis King (1884–1970), a carpenter of Polish origin who came to Montréal in 1906, settled in Saint-Lambert about 1931 and became one of its main builders. Between 1932 and 1951 he put up 70 to 100 houses of various styles chosen from the catalogues then in circulation, from neo-Tudor to postwar bungalows; the brick model "dérivant des cottages anglais" that stands out is what the town now calls the King Cottage. The 2019 study identifies five families of King houses (two-slope roof with Tudor porch; Tudor gable to the street; two-slope classical; hipped classical; bungalow).
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 8

phase_title: Postwar modern — the bungalow boom and Préville
principal_cladding: stone; artificial-stone; clay-brick; wood; roughcast; metal-siding
siting_landscape: The single-storey bungalow with carport or garage "fait fureur" in the 1950s and 60s, when Saint-Lambert boomed; mostly standardised plans, some architect-designed one-offs.
massing: Rectangular or articulated plan, one level (de plain-pied) or two storeys, often with garage or carport; flat roof or low slopes, sometimes inverted, variously oriented. | Few projections: overhanging eaves, marquises and bay windows are frequent; some angular façades with advances and recesses; massive chimneys often the only vertical element.
articulation: Generally no applied ornament; asymmetrical composition stressing horizontal lines; façade "mosaics" made by the arrangement, textures and colours of brick, stone and wood; occasional worked-metal railings or grilles, ceramic insertions or colour panels.
openings: Doors of varied models, solid or glazed; patio doors for the rear; garage doors sober and matched to the front door. | No standard window; size and type vary by room; glass-block openings frequent.
materials: Natural or artificial stone (concrete), brick, wood, roughcast, metal siding, often combined. | Asphalt shingle entirely suitable on pitched roofs.
conservation: Imitation materials (engineered wood such as Canexel, vinyl, plastics) proscribed. | Wood windows may be replaced in aluminium or PVC provided the opening mode (crank, guillotine, sliding) matches the original. | Do not add ornament; preserve the stripped look. | Do not raise foundations or change the roof form; side/rear reduced-volume additions only.
blurb_en: The postwar house: bungalow or two-storey box, garage or carport built in, low or flat roof, big windows sized to the room behind them, glass block by the door, a massive chimney as the one vertical. No ornament; the mosaic of stone, brick and wood is the décor.
origin_en: Modernism via the Bauhaus and the Chicago School, reacting against ornament-laden historicism; its commonest domestic form, the bungalow, "devenu le modèle d'habitation dominant après la Seconde Guerre mondiale" with the baby boom, suburbanisation and easier access to property and the car. In Saint-Lambert some 700 houses went up in the five years after the war; Préville, created 1948 and annexed 3 May 1969, is the western extension of that boom.
photo_credit: © Ville de Saint-Lambert / Patri-Arch (G. Mongrain, M. Dubois), Répertoire des courants architecturaux, fiche 10
